PRACTICAL POULTRY FARMING.
(By Redcap.)
POULTRY FOR EXHIBITION. (Continued). MUNN°.

Nearly every variety of eihibition fowls requires shading from the weather. In the case of white fowls most especially. If they are not protected from sun and rain, they soon love their natural colour. And once they do you can never get it back until they have moulted. Therefore you should lose no time to separating from the young at, ck any likely show specimens. It is chiefly the light cokured varieties which suffer most in this direction. Perham you have noticed for instance, a Barred Rock looking somewhat brassy in top colour. Well ! This is always caused by being too frequently subjected to weather conditions. Now while it is chiefly the light colours which buffer moet,black fowls also suffer but in a less degree. The only difference is that the former need closer protection then do the latter. White show birds can only be kept pure in colour by artifi- cial shelter, while on the other band, Buff, Black, and the Laced varieties can be kept almoat perfect in colour when naturally shaded. All this goes to prove the neceeeity of having plenty of trees and shrubs planted in the runs. To return to the white fowle,they should be housed in a ovable and bottomless runs. So that, while Laing moteetrd limn the weather,they may --et the same time—live almost under natural con- ditions. &undness in ,ulour moots for a great deal in the show pen, what-ver the variety may he.
PREPARING FOU 111 K SHIII

White fowls of c• urea needs bath ere they are fit for the 'boards 'and under no consideration what- ever should the amateur attempt this process until he has practised ran common fowl. Let me instruct you how to proceed. First of all the fowl should have the legs well washed. Let the legs souk in fairly but water then with an ordio ary nail bruit/land soap, scrub well until you have removed all the dirt from about the scales. After v. u have done thin, place the bird in the pen white you make further preparations. Get three good sized baths ; fill the first with hot water into which has been dissolved I packet of " Luz." The second one should contain water not quite as hots, the first and without soap at all. The third one should contain bike-warm water, to which has been added a small quantity of ordinary washing blue ; and with the asmstance of an attendant you may procesd. Thoroughly soak the whole body with the soapy w.tter, continue to work the soapy trate into the feathers with both hands ttntil you are satisfied that all dirt aud stains are ri moved. Then carefully lift the fowl into the second bath and rinse cut every particle of the soapy water. After you have done no. give the final rinse in the blue water, then let the fowl be free to have a good shake. Then place it its an unlined sluts bask, t before it boinbt fire Keep it free from draughts lout do not let it he too near the fire. When the ' victim ' is thoroughly dry it is a good plan to let it fly how • fairly high perch several times. By this method it straightens r at the webbing of the feather.. Now all this should be done at least three days before the show so that the fowl may have time to - a sort of reacclimatiso. There is not the least dr übt hut that aucb an ordeal is very trying to the fowl which undergees such an unusual process After the amateur has practised on • common fowl after such a manner as I have described, he may venturer on one intended fur ealtibitien. Oat is of course if the trial proved a success. If not, then try again until you have thoronghly mastered the art. Before finally dispatching the bird to a show, the face, comb and legs should be gently rubbed vu r with a sponge which has been soaked in a few drop. of glycerine and cucumber. After so doing gently stroke the feathers from load to tail with a silk handkerchief and the work is complete. It is a long story. Nevertheless, if you want to pt your birds down in tip-top ' condition, every detail is absolutely necessary.

It is not advieable for backyorders to attempt rear- ing large fowls for exhibition purpose.. The area is too limited, and if it is the denim e of the backyarder to enter the fancy, he should do so with bantams. It is surprising how well the ' midgets' thrive in a small ran if kept clean and div. Keeping fancy bantams is a vote inteteeting and fascinating hobby ; and further, it is profitable if you shot with the right strain. good specimens fetch just as high an average price as most of he larger varieties. They coat little to Keep and they cost little to exhibit. For this moon, you only wed small show baskets ; therefore the railway rates are kw, and, in fact, if you ecnfine your efforts to local event., you can without much trouble convey a sniall tram to a show,with the aid of • bicycle. I know one prominent bantam fancier who, often enough, tarries his show bird• to different events after this fashion. Almcst at y variety of bottoms will do well in town runs. They stand con- finement well, and once o beer nie on adherent to bantam. as a hobby, it is only with great reluctance that you would gire them tip. There is always a good demand for morphia stock, because bantams are much sought after for children's pets. It is then with (very confidence that I advise my readers—whose scare is limited- to go in for b...ntams ass hobby.

In concluding these articles en exhibition poultry I hare bf no means exhausted the subject. A great deal more can profitably be said, lent I am afraid that my utility friends will he on my track for neglecting them so long. However, let me say to these who intend making a wart, don't be misled by purchasing at random. First if all understand the variety you intend taking up. Then make the acquaintance of a reliable breeder; keep in close tench with him; follow the show e' ports, and visit as many as you can with convenience. Stick to your breed ; Specialize ! Specialize!! Specialize ! !! until you have made a name. The laurels will surely follow, and lam cettsin that if you follow my advice to the letter, your hobby will become a profitable pleasure. Do i.therivise, and you will give up in disgust. There is an art in raising and showing successfully good birds of any breed. You must

But they will come by patient waiting it you will only plod along in the way which I have tried to point out to you in thews articles or. Exhibition Poultry. _SOO4OOATILE NOTES.. .

Egcs now ars fairly plentiful —Sind you should have no difficulty in obtaining them for sitting purposes. You may continue to hatch from the lighter varietiea. By this time you should have hatched out the bulk from the heavier breeds. However, if you intend to further increase the stock no time should be lost, bennune it takes them no much longer to niatuie than the Mediterranean breeds. That is, of course, if you want rollers for winter laying. (let all the eggs down you possibly can from the table fowls. These if hatched in April or May will make fire birds for Christmas.
THE TOE'. 9T1,4 K.

No time should be lost in separating the early hatched youngsters. y this time they will be fairly well developed and as a result of being separated they will thrive much quicker. Don't feed them on fond which will force them. Keep them backward until they me well developed. Leghorns especially are very precocious and if care is not used they come on to Ivy at too early an age, and thereby they become stunted in growth. Therefore, to prevent this keep tl em on • diet of good hard wheat and not to much soft fond. It always pays in the long run to encourage full body development before exciting the action of the ovary. That is one reason why you should separate this class of fowl as soon as possible. an i always as aeon as the sexes can be determined.

Aso jet look-not for .;erniin in the to ung stock is essential at this season of the year. You should freely dust the sent boxes and especially the nests of broody hens. A tin tf Neatings is worth its weight in gold in the poultry yard and ran. Examine your stock at night time, and with the aid of an attendant sire each one a thorough dusting with the poordcr. It not only adds to the comfort of your fowls, bet also pays in the egg yield. Fowls irfe,ted with lice can- not be expected to yield to the same extent as those which are kept cies.

div.head: " MACBETH."
div.p: " MACBETH."
COMMEMORATION PERFORMANCE AT WARRINGTON

The much-discussed and eagerly-awaited , performance of" Macbeth" by local amateurs , in commemoration of Shakespeare's birth took place on Monday evening at the Royal Court Theatre. One hardly needs to add that the building was orowded in every part by an enthusiastic audience, for so much was certain and obvious a full week earlier. Mr.C. D.Law's ambitiou project aroused uncommon interest right from its inception, and with the Infirmary as the beneficiary object, generous patronage was always assured. Of the performance itself, we may say honestly and unreservedly that its complete- ness and quality were a pleasant surprise. Mr. Law and his friends aimed high in their histrionic aspirations, and when the choice of" Macbeth" for a one-night performance became known, there were many keen I enthusiasts for the drama who had mis- givings, lest "vaulting ambition " might o'erleap itself and the hastily-gathered com- pany fail to do justice both to Shakespeare and the greatest of his tragedies. Monday night laid all such doubtings at rest. The players largely discounted inexperience, and gave a true and worthy rendering of the soul-racking drama which merited the warmest praise. There were, inevitably, lapses and inequalities which no amount of mere rehearsing could eliminate, and some of these may require special reference later on, but we wish to be perfectly clear in our expres- sion of satisfaction with the success which was undoubtedly achieved. In Mrs.R.Garnett the company found a Lady Macbeth who satisfied every beholder with her dramatic insight and powerful characterisation. Mrs. Garnett was lifted right out of herself by the exigencies of so great a role, and triumphed over some slight physical dis- abilities in a way which compelled admira- tion. For instance, she possesses a voice, the soft inflections of which are essentially unsuited to the declamation of the passionate utterances of Lady Macbeth when she has to nerve her vacillating lord to the bloody crime against the sleeping King Duncan. Yet she was commanding to. a degree not anticipated, and the scene lacked nothing in grim realism and forcefulness on her account. Fine indeed was her nervous and mental triumph when Macbeth reeled from the chamber of death with his deed but half-done, and the frail-woman was sub- jugated to the expediency of the dread moment by her own iron will. Again, in the sleep-walking scene, Mrs. Garnett surprised us all with the depth of the poignant anguish she inarticulately but vividly expressed. She was as pitiable as she had heretofore been majestic, and ratified a distinct claim to be ranked as no mean tragedienne. Mr. Law's " Macbeth " was an almost equal triumph. lacking solely something of the quality of restraint. At times we thought him a little too ' frenzied, but his interpretation evidenced independent reading and study which were alike creditable and interesting. Throughout, Mr. Law was word-perfect, and considering that he was largely concerned with the heavy business of stage-management, he gave a ; remarkable rendering of apart which tried to ; the uttermost considel able histrionic powers. With so striking and dramatic a presence, Macbeth was doubtless difficult to play up to, and one or two members of the company seemed to suffer by comparison. Mr. H. M. Ashton, as Banquo, a chieftain of equal rank and importance, was overshadowed rather more than was desirable, and might perhaps have imparted more martial vigour into an otherwise excellent,well-spoken performar.ce. The Macduff of Mr. Harold Smith was one of the signal triumphs of the play. Voice, gesture, and deportment were admir- able, and we had as perfect a presentment of the warlike nobleman who brings low the ensanguined Macbeth as one need wish to see. Like Mr. Law,Mr. Harold ; Smith had his difficulties to contend with outside and apart from the pourtrayal of an ' exacting role. During the fight between himself and Macbeth at the close of the last act, the tragedy of a duel to the death was nearly turned to comedy by the excessive and noisy solicitude of the Tariff Reform ladies in the gallery for the safety of their political champion. Among the less distinc- tive parts, favourable mention must certainly be made of Mr. Henry Hallard's " porter, • which introduced bibulous comedy to a night-scene of grim import with artistic ; effect. The three witches (Mr. H. O. Adams Mr. Victor Roberts, and Mrs. Frank Griffiths) were extremely good. In make-up, cackling voice and weird mannerism, this horrific trio fulfilled admirably the supernatural part assigned them by the great dramatist who . penned the immortal tragedy of " Macbeth." ' They personally lacked not one single essential to appear as horribly witch- like as anything the imagination ' could conceive. Mr. H. G. Mosley was calm and dignified as King Duncan, but one can hardly imagine that the role was quite congenial to him. Compliments are the due, too, of Mr. Frank Richmond, , who spoke the meaning lines of Malcolm • with considerable effect for so young a player. The murderers (Messrs. Johnson ; and Hammond) were a realistically cut- throat pair, and very few of the other numerous characters who made briet individual incursions to the centre of the stage were lacking the power of self-efface- ment which only comes with diligent I rehearsal and painstaking coaching. It will ' perhaps be not untimely, at this point, to pay generous tribute to the immensity of Mr. , Law task and the truly admirably way in which he has achieved a high endeavour. The full cast of the company which ' he has brought through all the toil and trouble of an amateur performance of so great a play as" Macbeth" is as follows : Duncan, King of Scotland Mr H 0 Mosley btalcolm 1 „, Mr Frank Richmond Denalbein .1 Macbeth Generale of the King's... So far we have had nothing to say about the staging and stage-management. Both possessed features which attract-A notice. The staging was wholly admirable, and the numerous scenes have never been so well presented by any company which has occupied a Warrington stage. They com- bined the majesty and beauty which are so essential to any modern production of a Shakespearean trag3dy. It appeared to us that the stage-management was deficient in several respects, principally for the obvious reason that the faults were not discernible till the actual performance. In the two scenes where the witches hold their midnight incantations there was too much light, thus lessening the effect of eerie awsomeness which is so essential. By dispelling the dark- ness, much of the terror was also dispelled. Then, too, the setting of the banquet scene was open to much objection from our point of view. It is hardly conceivable that in a spacious banqueting hall the tables would be placed along walls so far apart, and the , guests huddled up against the cold stones. The arrangement left the floor clear for , Macbeth and his Queen, of course, which was a too obvious and stagey expedient. But the , greatest objection to the setting of tin whole • scene was apparent when Banquo's ghost ) appeared. The poor disembodied spirit of ' the murdered chieftain had to walk in right ) on the footlights, and appeared anything but I a credit to the other world with a white 3 veil over its pallid head and a pair of sub- stantial legs beneath. The apparition came , near to makings travesty of the whole scene f and was a sad fault in stagecraft. As a rule f Banquo's ghost appears behind the King's chair at the back of the stage, and distance • lends the requisite mystery and uncanniness to the vision. It would have been much I better if this more orthodox setting had ) been adhered to. These were the only notable ) blemishes in a highly creditable performance, . and if there is any repetition of the play - they could easily be amended. There was a I rather too full programme of music, • excellently played under the direction of Mr. • Boothrnyd. Shakespeare is sufficiently , enthralling to be independent of musical accessory, and a little less orchistration— ) subdued as it was—would have been an advantage during the most dramatic passazes. . . _

At the close there were repeated calls for Mr. Law, and he was accorded a deserving and flattering reception, to which he replied in a few well-chosen words which paid homage to the genius of the man whose anniversary they were celebrating and acknowledged the valuable helpof Mr. Loader, and the appreciation of the large audience. Finally there was a somewhat unnecessary and repeated call for Mr. Smith, who may perhaps have felt none too grateful for the perfervid enthusiasm of his friends. As is usual in amateur performances there are many acknowledgments due. The Com- mittee responsible for the production con- , sisted of Mr. Arthur Browne (chairman and hon. treasurer), Mr. Law, Mr. A. M. Loader, Mr. R. Garnett, Mr. F. G. Taylor and Mr. J. W. Bullen (hon. secretary). For the loan of scenery, armour, etc., and for help in many directions, the thanks of the Com- mittee are due to Mr. Joseph Beecham, Mr. Richard Flannagan (Manchester), Mr. F. R Benson, Mr. Henry Herbert, and Mr. A. M. Loader.

div.head: "LAW " AND THE PROPHETS.
div.p: THE "LAW " AND THE PROPHETS.
An Appreciation.
Lily Alfred Perris].

A smart critic, reviewing the original production of one of Bulwer Lytton's plays, •• Not so bad as we seem," declared it to be " Not no good as so expected." This criticism, notwithstanding the fact that very "great expectations " bad been ranied by laudatory and eulogistic fore-words, could not have been applied by the most hypercritical individual in the large audience assembled at the Royal Court Theatre, on !Jointly last —with any degree of uslice—to the twig. representatouol Shakespeare's great tragedy of " Macbeth " which was given by the company of amateur player., brought together tinder the aegis of Mr. Charles D. Law.

mise-en-scke so careful and resplendent, in all its details, with acting of a really high order and stage management chewing a uke disci imination throughout, the production deserved and achieved • complete and mqualified mimes.. Th. artistic ensemble and organic spirit were not lacking, and were, indeed, in a high degree, interesting, and the play has certainly never been mounted more magnifi- cently, or pis, ed by a more intelligent cast, before a Warrington audience. %%rinds clearly enunciated and the meaning matte fair ly understandable by correct emphasis, were to be appreciated for the compare ive rarity in the display of t hr 'equalities in professional performances which are not infr.quently served up to us—even in the present era of athuriced education. Not only were individual actors equal to their parts, but numerous little con- ceited effects of trouping and unnanement of the stage gave iile and spirit to the business of the scene, while the pictures pie beauty of the entire production remain• as a giateful memory if an inspiring and eventful mcamon, in the history of the Warrington Theatre.

Of course, there were outstanding features, and the audience vras not stow in inanifeeting it. satisfaction at the appearance or midi the achievements of particular favourites, lint it in somewhat to be regretted that a feeling, which it seemed impoesible entirely to suppress, should have made it difficult to appronie the enact proportions of approval which the artistic merit. of the performers called for—and received.

It was self-evident that tie predominant influence was the preponderance of the feminine element an the popular parts of the house—notahly in the pit— sad that soy large numbers of the good ladies were there for the pure gratification of seeing " our Harold" in his warpaint,taut with • somewhat defective appre- ciation of the poetic character of the pay. Let it he recorded, to the credit of the Member for Warrington, that hews, visibly perplexed lay the rersistent plaudits of his admirers on his initial entrance and that, like a true artiste, be abstained from any recognition of the embarrassing demonstration. From an artistic standpoint abne, the presence of so many who were apparently unsophisticated in the knowledge and understanding of such subtle reasoning as in exhibited in the characters of Macbeth and his wife—but in whom the risible faculty wan most prominent—was a distinct drawback to the perfect enjoyment by the more earnest end attentive &traitors of the play, in its entirety. Cons during the very crowded state of the theatre, however, and the mani- la at discomfort of many inn consequence, the writer in inclined to think that the compelling influonce of the undoubtedly p iwerful acting in many of the scenes— (very notably during Macduff's agonising moments as, and after, the news of the slaughter of his wife and children is hi oken to him, and again in the sleep- walking scene, by Lady Macbeth) to produce ntense and almost painful silence, under such circumstance., for quite a -lengthened period of time—affords the moat convincing evidence of the really extraordinary and conspicuous ability of the amateur artistes. To particularize, when no high a degree of

, excellence has been reached by many of the principal performer., appears invidious, and the writer would have been glad if he could have found a may of escape from this dilemma. but not having succeeded, he decides to, metaphorically, bracket the two chief actor., Messrs. Charles Law and Harold Smith, as Senior Wianglers, and the chief aubstitute actress for lady Mrs. Robert Garnett, as above the Senior Wi Ingle's. .. . . . .. _

The gentlemen are both exceptionally fine actor.; :as amateurs of course—and are worthy of all the praise and commendation that can be bestowed upon them, but the writer cannot stay to dwell upon their performances more specificallynntil he has divcharged what he conceives to be his manifest duty, and accordingly be" here maketh bold declaration " that the outstanding feature of this very remarkable production was the truly wonderful and eminently consistent pourtrayal of the character of ready Macbeth by Mrs. Robert Garnett. Viewed front an artistic standpoint only, and without the slightevt particle of personal interest or populsr feeling (for the writer has nut even a sufficient knowledge of any , one of the chief members of the cast to enable him t recognise them off the stage, with the single exception .1 Mr. Smith, whom Ile saw and heard once only in October or November last, at Parr he unhesitatingly affirms that the realization for us,of this marvellous creation of the poet's genius by Mrs. Garnett is the most notable event In the range of (amateur) tragic acting which has come within his experience, extending over clout on half a century, during which he Las had a very real intimicy with histrionics, both amateur and professional, and with the remembrance still fresh in his mind of a long roll of memorable insprsonations of the pest he has been privileged to witness including Mrs. Charles Roan, Miss Cushman, Miss Marriott, Mrs Charles Calvert, Mrs. Hermann Veain, besides many others. The art that can conceal the art, by which an assumption is mad., to produce the effect of reality upon our senses, is a rain posseeftion indeed. Mrs. Garnett posse/wee it and exercises this wonderful charm upon her audience to a degree most surprising when it is considered that she Las had only occasioeal opportunities of practising that art which, nut infrequently, • lifetime's cmstant experience hardly succeeds in perfecting. The writer regrets that since will not permit him to dissect or to analyse the acting fully in this issue of the paper though lie hors 10 du so in a subsequent i.e. the autopsy being thtroaghly independent, diselmea features, pr svibly, which may not have appealed to the observation of tho-e who have alrmdy Lad the oppv.tunity of express,ng their opiei

THE EXAMINER.
SAMRDAY. APRIL 29 1911.
The Referendum was
THE GAME OF introduced to the MAKE-BELIEVE. English public in an

accidental and casual manner. But this must not lead anybody to think that it is not a good subject for make-believe. It is in reality excellent for that purpose. When he was making a long speech in favour of the Referendum on Wednesday, Mr. CAVE may have failed to remember that when he had last said anything about it he roundly declared its unsuitability for English use. He may have blushed a little when Mr. HERBERT SAMUEL reminded him of his former opinion, but probably: his amour propre was restored by Sir William Anson, who is a great authority on the Constitution, and who approved and disapproved of the Referen- dum practically in the same breath. The Referendum would be a formidable and two- edged weapon said SIR WILLIAM. It might be serious in its operation in several ways, The Tory party favours it, he asserts, because it is unwilling to Bee the foundations of the Constitution altered by a precarious majority. It is to " save the Constitution that the Conservative party wishes to sweep the Constitution away! If there were any gods of the kind believed in by the Greek and Roman poets, how they would laugh at the simple cunning of men like Mr. CAVE and SIR WILLIAM ARSON!

If we thought it necessary to prove that the Referendum has been adopted by the Opposition as a mere controversial device we should be content to rest the case on the speeches which were made in its favour in the House of Commons. Take Mr.BALFOUR, for instarce. The Referendum, he said, is an instrument to be carefully applied. There must be RO frequent use of it. Any Government must be most careful as to its application. And so on. We may affirm, with the utmost confidence, that the Refer- endum would not be again heard of if the Opposition were to-morrow, by some piece of wizardry, to find itself seated on the right hand of the SPEAKER and once more admin- istering the affairs of the realm. The leader of the Opposition assured the House that the Referendum was under consideration by himself and his friends months before the last General Election. He did not add, as he might have done, that the result was the publication by the Central Tory organisation of a thorough condemnation of the Referen- dum, lock, stock, and barrel.

What is going on in regard to this matter is greatly calculated to alienate serious- minded men from politics. The make- believe is really too aggressively-transparent. We are 'coming to "the end of all things," says Lord ROSEBERY, because it is proposed to deprive the House of Lords of its absolute veto. What is the counterproposal? It is to smash, destroy, and pulverise the prin- ciple and practice of representative govern- ment! The Referendum, said Mr. ASQUITH, is revolutionary. It is, indeed. It is revolutionary to the last degree. It would make legislation on the present lines wholly impossible. Members of Parliament would be representative no longer. They would he something with lees independence even than delegates. It is nonsense for Mr. BALFOUR to say that the Referendum would be brought into use only now and again. If it were used at all it would and must be in use almost constantly. This, we believe, is so well understood that no party would advocate the incorporation of such a system into the Constitution of this country if there were any genuine belief that the thing would be done. It is just because all parties would
run away from the proposal if there were a danger of its taking practical shape that the Opposition regards it as such an exceedingly pretty toy to play with.

Like the poor, the THE INFIRMARY. Infirmary we have always with us. The final appeal" for the completion of the Million Penny Fund has been issued this week. A further £1,600 is required and towards this,£soo has already been subscribed by donations, a list of which is printed on our front page. They include a cheque for fifty guineas from Mr. A. E. Davies, of Edinburgh, a gentleman whose generosity would be somewhat puzzling were it not made known that he is the son of Dr. John Davies, who formerly practised in Warring- ton and occupied the old house in Sankey - street, now known 88 the residence of Mr. 'Charles White. Mr. Davies is a life governor of the Infirmary, and we hope his keen, though detached, interest in the Institution will prove a healthy stimulus to Warringtonians at home.

Nothing could be more LIBERAL gratifying to the friends ENTHUSIASM, of progress in Warring- ton than the energy and enthusiasm with which the work of perfecting the local Liberal organization is proceeding. There is a healthy determina- tion that the next election, whenever it comes, shall find every section of the party thoroughly prepared to regain Warrington's allegiance to the cause of the people which received such splendid endorsement from the country in December, but which, unfor- tunately, suffered a temporary check in this constituency. The Liberal Women's Associa- tion in particular is distinguishing itself by the thoroughness and spontaneity of its methods of re-organization, and already a highly encouraging spirit of optimism pre- vails. The series of ward meetings brought to a close last evening has demonstrated the fact that the Association has at its command in all parts of the town an earnest body of workers who may be relied upon to do their utmost to ensure the triumph of Liberalism. The gatherings held in St. John's and Latchford Wards this week were honoured with the presence of Mr. and Mrs. A. H. Crosfield who were agreeably impressed with the warmth of the welcomes accorded to them. Mr. Crosfield's hopeful addresses put in terse and homely phrases the debt which the women of England owe to the Liberal Government for their social legisla- Aion and the supreme importance of resisting the repeated efforts of the Conservatives to fasten the disastrous policy of Protection and food taxes upon the working class.

Warrington is becom- THE HEALTH OF ing a healthy town, THE BOROUGH, and no doubt much of the credit is due to the Health Committee, which has shown increased activity in recent years under the 'spur of an awakening public opinion and an -energetic medical officer. Dr. J. Coote Hibberfs fourth annual report, just to hand, 'contains a vast amount of information and statistical analysis and comparison relative to public health affairs, which is of -the utmost value. The best thing the Medical Officer has to tell us is that the .general and infantile death rates of the I Borough for the year 1910 are the lowest ever recorded, viz. : 154 and 113, against -averages for the 77 great towns of 14'3 and 115. When it is remembered that the great towns quoted for comparative reasons include -several reputed health resorts it will be more clearly seen that Warrington's death-rate is particularly low for an industrial centre. It is especially gratifying to see that such a marked improvement in the infantile death- rate, which only five years ago was 156 per 1,000 births, and in 1893 stood at the appallingly high figure of 208 per 1,000. Warrington has realised its past " blood- guiltiness " (to quote Alderman Bennett's famous phrase) in the matter of child-life .and the increased energy now being applied to the improvement of sanitation and housing should bear further gratifying results.

There is one particular INFECTED MILK danger to the infant life of Warrington which Dr. Hibbert alludes to in grave terms, and which has previously been the subject of comment in these columns. We refer to tuberculous milk, which finds its way into the borough in very large quantities. The Medical Officer states that bacteriological examination shows that 8 out of 41 dairy farmstad been supplying tuberculous milk to the borough, and these eight farms have between them sent in an estimated quantity of 2,800 pints of infected milk daily. This is an alarming revelation, and unfortunately -the Legislature only arms municipal authori- ties with very cumbersome machinery for checking such a widespread evil. Efficient, frequent and compulsory veterinary , inspection of cows in all dairy farms will do much to save the children, and save the often innocent farmers from themselves. It is to be hoped that an early amendment of the law will be procurable by the joint action of municipal and urban authorities. Mean- while, the only safeguard is for all milk to be boiled before use—a precaution we can expect only a very small proportion of mothers and housewives to take. So far as lies in its power we hope the Health Com- mittee of Warrington and its officers will take every possible step to discover and trace all supplies of infected milk which may be sent into the borough. The cost of investi- gation and analysis is of no account compared with the extreme urgency of the situation from a public health point of view.

The Belfast correspondent of the "Morn- ing Post" telegraphs: The sum of £lOO,OOO has been subscribed to pay the expenses of the great anti-Home Rule campaign, and the Unionist Association of Ireland will meet in Dublin to put the finishing touches to the elaborate arrangements for the campaign. It is expected that by the beginning of May the first batch of speakers and canvassers will have left Ireland for England and Scotland.

Some of our readers have inquired whether it was "free trade" or" fair trade" which influenced Lady Greenall to purchase the Mayoress's gold chain in London, and to employ a Viennese band (from London) for the entertainment of her guests. After the 'Tariff Reform League's shop-window display of home-made goods, and Her Ladyship's keen interest therein, we should have expected Warrington orders for Warrington workers. There are both goldsmiths and musicians in the good old town!

"Out of the mouths of babes and sucklings"! A member of the Warrington Town Council the other day put several questions to a bright little boy of five years, who attends the Bolton School. In answer to one query the youngster said proudly and confidently "I can swim like a bird." "But birds do not swim," said the teacher standing by. "My bird's a duck " said the self-possessed youngster—and the story is now one of the cherished possessions of the Alderman in question.

According to the ;Hai rates for the differ- ent wards in the town, as printed in the Medical Officer's annual report, Latchford and St. Austin's are the healthiest wards. Their general and infantile death rates are the lowest of the nine wards, and are almost identical. Bewsey, St. John's, and Howley are the three wards where life seems cheapest and these are well-known to include the most congested parts of the town. Expansion, sanitation and fresh air are the only remedies, and unfortunately 'their application is only sl2w..

" • Mr. Philip Snowden, M.P., says in this week's " Christian Commonwealth" : The unblushing way which the Government continue to give fat jobs at the public expense to Pleir friends is becoming a public scandal of serious moment. There are two by-elections pending at present, both came d by the appoiet- ment of Liberal M.P.'s to 'office of profit "under under . .

the CrAvn. The one is the appointment of Major Guest to the post of Liberal Whip. Upon which the only comment necessary (says the " Westminster Gazette ") is that Major Guest's salary in his "fat" job is nil! He is a Junior Lord of the Treasury,and as such holds in theory an " office of profit " under the Crown. As a fact, however, only three ' Junior Lords are paid salaries, and Major Guest is not one of them. • • Preaching on Sunday at the re-opening of Waverton Church, near Wigton, the Bishop of Carlisle advanced a strong plea for cottage gardens and flower cultivation. He wished from the bottom of his heart, he said, England might some day arrive at a point when every householder owned his own house with, as far as possible, a little holding or garden attached. His Lordship denotuiced extravagant expenditure upon flowers at funerals, and said that when in New York he remembered that at one funeral between £2OO and £3OO was spent on flowers—mostly sent out of pride and show, and because of fashion. Extravagance was sin, and extravagant expenditure on funerals gener- ally was wrong. When his turn came to die, he hoped that money would not be spent and wasted upon his funeral. Let the money be given to the poor and sick, and let it be a simple and reverent funeral. The Spring Assembly of the Baptist Union of Great Britain and Ireland was opened on Monday, at the Bloomsbury Central Church. Sir George W. Macalpine (Accrington), the retiring president, introduced his successor, ..'rincipal W. Edwards (Cardiff). The Council, in their report for the year ended December 31st, stated that there had been a decrease in church membership of 3,775, and in Sunday scholars of 2,794. Churches had increased in number by 18, chapels by 21, Sunday school scholars by 522, local preachers by 40, and pastors in charge by 12, while fresh seat- ing accommodation had been provided for 17,616 persons. The receipts for the year totalled £23,638, and the amount distributed to ministers and widows from the Annuity Fund, and to the pastors and churches, aided by the Home Work and Education Funds, reached a total of over £13,500. • • Principles, unless they are popular, do not seem to command much respect on the War- rington Board of Guardians. The Rev. A. M. Mitchell, at Wednesday's annual meeting quite conscientiously and justifiably pro- tested against the re-election of Mr. E. L. Bent, on the ground that he is connected with the drink traffic, and as a result oecame the butt of several members' ribaldry. There was much reason and force in the rev, gentleman's objection. A considerable proportion of the members of the Assessment Committee (appointed by the Guardians) are also connected with the Trade, and not unnaturally they view sympathetically the applications of brewers and licensees for reductions of assessments even when the professional advisers of the Committee are against them. The result is a loss in rateable value, which has to be borne by the general body of ratepayers who are fully assessed. The same thing has occurred in Manchester (as in Warrington to the extent of a penny rate). Mr. R. B. Batty, an authority on the question, says: "It is another instance of how the trade hare defeated the objects of the Legislature and , thrown the burden on the irneral body politic; ' the intention of Parliament has been defeated by the trade. The obvious lesson is that the public should see the trade do not steal a march upon the.,, again." The Rev, A. M. Mitchell's attitude on the matter is consistent with sound public policy, and will have plenty of support out- side if not inside the Board Room of the Warrington Guardians.

div.head: PALACE AND HIPPODROME.
div.p: PALACE AND HIPPODROME.

This week there is a surfeit of comedians at the Palace arid Hippodrome; lint despite their ingenuity Sammy Sid Ida stands rot. He is reputed to is a born humorist and one cannot dispute this; tor from the moment lie steps on the platform until the moment he leaves, the audience is convulsed with laughter. its is there to enjoy himself and when Ile apparently spontaneorely introduces jokes into his remarks lie laughs quite as much as hie bearers, Ile in not like his brother Scotsmen inasmuch as when they crack a joke they oten fail to notice it. On Monday evening as an encore he impersonated an exci ed football enthusiast watching the cop final and the manner in which lie knocked his fellow apectstors about was fine fun. A sketch entitled "Capita" contributed by Jan Iludenyi, the actor violinist, Mr. Drew Mackintosh ru,d Miss llilda Stewart was very entertaining, not only on account of its original conception but because of the charming music rendered by Jan Itudenli. Ile is, indeed, a skilful exponent of the •iolin and is well worth listening to, no matter how fastidious one might be. The— Enter Trio are capital entertainere. Soule wonderful joggling is presented •nd their efforts are much appreciated, but the Jujitsu exhibition by Miss Clarice and one of the soldiers is fascinating. Royal Togo delights the audience with spinning lops and bin slide from the roof to the stage blindfolded with Iris head in a sack is charecterintic of the daring Japanese rare. As • six feet if comicality Walter Emerson is superb. His songs are far from stereo- typed and the accompanying gesticulations are laughable. Crvennie Haste in quaint songs and fancy dances merits the frequent applause she receives, and Andre Burn, described as comedian and epeciality ecccentric dancer, fulfils the description. The pictures are good,and some pleasing items are rendered by the orchestra under the leadership of Mr. E. A. Widdop

div.head: MATINEE CONCERT AT THE HIPPODROME
div.p: MATINEE CONCERT AT THE HIPPODROME

The concert on Monday afternoon in which Mr... Arthur Newstead a well-known pianist and an excellent party of vocalists and instrumentalist. were ' announced to take part, happened at a singularly unt rtunate moment for the artiates themselvea an well as for thoie of our townsmen who might have been expected to have formed a numerous audience. In addition to a function of exceptional interest taking place at the Town Hall the concert was overshadowed by the impending Macbeth redo:mance around which great public interest bad gathered. S, it is not altogether surprising that a mere handful of people assembled to listen to the matinee programme. Nor did misfortunes come singly. Wh thee themeagrenes. of the attendance had to do with the indispc.ition of two of the artistes in the way of cause and effect, we know not, but it was peculiarly unfortunate that out of a party of four prominent musicians two should fall out in quite an unforeseen way. Nevertheless Mr. Newstead and Madame Sobrino took up,n themselves the heavy work of carrying through an afternoon's programme,gaining thereby awl, enthitainstie applause as a slender arid not ungrateful audience could proffer. The fascinating historical records, the architectural beauty and picturesque situation of St. o.ald's • Church, Winwick, mike it one of the most interesting churches in the Warrington district. Its association Wllll some of the mo 4 sti• ring periods of English life - notably with the civil war, when Winwiek was the scene of decisive engagements and Royalists sought refuge in the church—has no often been written about, that a very brief outline of the church's history will suffice here. The reference to "St. Oswald of the same viii " in the Itornestlay Book gives us the first I mention of the church. The Domesday Survey was niade iu 1080. and it is supposed that the church was the gift of Roger of Poictou, the Norman to whom this part if Lancashire was given. The present building dates from 1358, hut Ins been variously improved and enlarged. The chancel was rebuilt in 1845 and was the stuck of Pugin. Among die treasutes of the church inns ancient and beautiful rood screen. The venerable If net tr of the chnrch (the Rev. Canon Oswald By. Leycester Penrhyn, MA is greatly beloved by litt parishioners and, in audit i n to his parochial dutiesdie takesa prominent and much appreciated part in church activities in die Liverpool diocese. Canon Penrhyn graduated at Balliol College, Oxford, and was onlained deacon in 1852 and pi ieat in 1853. His first curacy w. at Upton St. Leonard's from 1852 to 18.211 and became to Winwick ins similar capacity in 1850. Next lie was curate at Bickerstafle and became Vicar of Huyton in 1809. Ile was appointed Rector of Winwick in 1890 uod his work in the parish has Leen attended with much success. A few yearn ago the south portion of the Church was rebult at a cost of .114.1100, of which £2,0111) was raised by the parishioners and £2,000 wan advanced by the Ecclesiaatiaal Commissioners. Canon Penrhyn has been an honorary canon of Liverpool Cathedral since 1889 and chaplain to the Biabop of Liverpotl since 1901. From 1887 to 1910 he teas • proctor for the Archrleaconry of Warrington and for many year. he held the important position if Rural Dean of Winwick.

div.head: Visit to India. Elsa Broadbent's Lecture at St. George's Mission.
div.p: A Visit to India. Elsa Broadbent's Lecture at St. George's Mission.

A most interestinc, ant highly instructive lecture mop delivered by Miss Broadbent to a large audience at St. George's klitutioo on Tuesday evening, on her experiences in Indix, during recent visit. The lecture was illustrated with lantern slides from photographe taken by the lecturer's mister. The Bev. Canon Willis presided. After a short account pf the vot age, the cturer went on to speak of her impressions of Calcutta and of the tremendous heat experienced in going through the lied Sm. Special attention mu paid to the places which figured prominently in the tragic history of Ile Indian Mutiny. In describing the religious customs of the country, Mist; Broadbent said that Gm dead were disposed of on tie banks of the river Ganged!, the body of a man being wrapped ins white robe and that of a woman in a scarlet robe. 'the body nog first dinned in the stater sod left for some time with its feet in the water, afterwards I eing burned on the funeral pyre. The ashes were afterward, scattered in the flanges. This practice of burning the dead wee molt sanitary in such a hot country, although it ought to be stripped of its barbarous ceremony. The lecturer said the Indian woman couldahanie a European woman for movement, of grace in walking. div.head: St John's Presbyterian Church. The Rev. W Reid on Prayer.
div.p: St John's Presbyterian Church. The Rev. W Reid on Prayer.

Preaching ot St. John'. 011 Sunday evening, the Rev. Wm. Reid dealt with the subject of the • Reasonable- nem. of Prayer," taking for his text I. Them chap. 6, verse 17th. " Pray without ceasing." They did not follow Paul very far, paid Mr. Reid, before Ciey found him breaking away from the argument he was pursuing In order to exhort to the holy ministry of prayer. "Pray without refining" Wllll his great advice to the Christian friends to whom he addreesed his lettere In the present times they asked thorn. selves %hat should they pray for, but thet ques- tion never suggested itself in the ler back days to their fathers, who moved ateatt in the great places of God's love and presence, and acknowledged no boundaries. Science had made known the rigid and inflexible laws which govern the forces of nature, and to pray for anything which would interfere with those forces might seem Iropoehible. That there wan in nature no room fir prayer was a statement often hurled at the heads of Curietian men end women who believed in the power and reaaonahleness of prayer, but one of the greatest scientists of the day said that science lard revealed nothing which need debar them front praying unto God. Ilrit,after all,whet was nature hod what dl they really know about it ? Take their own bodies for example. They knew that by the influence of thought alone the body might become either hot or cold without anything external being brought into crmtact with it. Tbst being ponsible wee it unreasonable to sappose that the great mind and heart of Chid, which was at the centre of the universe, srao unable to work a miraele in Ilia one body, which they alright, without irreverence, call Nature ? Was there anything unreesonable in God drawing away the rain from one part and scattering it in another ? What was there to hinder the great Mind, especially when the human thought and prayer goes forth with all the intensity of the human soul behind it, end COMea into union with the great heart and thought of trod who in turn responds as lie does, and couples His great mind with the small finite mind of naarkend tr.gether human and divine nperst• ? Tuerefore, might they not 811 y on their fathers wed to any" There is nothing we will keep hack from God ; what we want we will ask for without doubt in our 'nimbi."

- - - - Prince Henry of Prussia, brother of the Kaiser, and Grand Admiral of the. German davy, who with his Consort will form part of the large circle of royal guests from abroad at King George's Coronation, is a sailor and a sportsman, and enjoys great personal popularity both in Germany and in this country, where he has several times been a welcome visitor, Prince Henry is 48 years old. Princess Henry of Prussia was born Princess Irene Of Hesse-Dwentadt, daughter of our own Princess Alice of Hesse, and consequently a granddaughter of Queen Victoria. Her marriage with Prin... Henry took place during the hist few weeks of the Emperor Frederick's life, and was one of the last functions attended by him. She is fond of riding, driving, and yachting, and knows how to use a girt, am accomplishment acquired in Scc*land.

div.head: ANTIQUARIAN : CHAPTERS.
div.p: ANTIQUARIAN : CHAPTERS.
GORDON'S MEMORY.
Unknown Episode io Gs Hero s Life.
By &she? Weldon, Dean of Manchester.

The memory of the great Cotton Famine in 1862 still hangs a shadow over Macchester and the circle of large boroughs which lie around it and invest it with its unique com- mercial and political influence. It accounts in a considerable measure for the present devotion of South-east Lancashire to Free Trade. For the Civil War, which had broken out the year before in the United States of America had produced an incalculable amount of poverty and misery in the cotton- spinning districts of England. It is difficult after the lapse of nearly fifty years to realise all that was involved in the sudden and entire cessation of the supply of the raw material upon which the operatives of Lancashire were dependent for their daily bread. Within a few weeks the amount of pauperism doubled at Bury, Oldham, and Rochdale; it increased three-fold at Man- chester and Burnley, four-fold at Stock- port, five-fold at Ashton-under-Lyne, and there was every reason to fear that the limit of distress had not even then been nearly reached.

The story of the Cotton Famine, painful as it is, is yet redeemed not only by the noble generosity with which all classes of the com- munity, the poor as much as the rich, in the South no less than in the North of England, came to the rescue of the starving operatives, but by the calm and cheerful fortitude which the operatives themselves exhibited in the dark days of their heavy trial. The late Mr. Molesworth, in his "History of England," says :—" It was remarkable that during the enforced temperance of this period there was a marked diminution in the number of deaths throughout the districts most affected by the famine. Another satisfactory circumstance attending it was the establishment of schools for the instruction of adults, who gladly devoted the time thus placed at their disposal to procur- ing for themselves that elementary educa- tion which they had not been able to obtain in their youth. Sewing schools were also established in all parts of the manufacturing Idistricts, by which that most useful but I hitherto much-neglected branch of female education was taught; so that many a Iwoman who had previously been unable to !mend a hole in her child's shirt, before the conclusion of the famine became an accom- plished semptress, able to instruct her own daughters in the useful art she had thus acquired. In this and in many other ways good came out of evil, and the famine left behind it beneficial as well as injurious traces." (Volume III.; page 203.)

div.head: DARK LANK -SCHOOL.
div.p: DARK LANK -SCHOOL.

Among the sewing schools so opened at that time was one in a poverty-stricken part of Manchester, which bore then, as it bears to-day, the ominous name of Dark-lane. A city missionary, Mr. James Johnson, a member of the committee which had estab- lished this sewing school and others in the same neighbourhood, was struck end grieved by the number of the children who for want of clothes or some other reason, were attend- ing no Sunday school, but were running wild and often nearly naked about the streets. He was moved, like Robert Raikes of Gloucester, with a strong desire to save them from barbarism. There happened to be at the corner of Dark-lane a small upper room generally used as a storeroom for cotton, but left vacant owing to the cotton famine. Mr. Johnson obtained leave from the firm by whom the room was occupied to make use of it until it should be needed for business again. There he opened a ragged school in the winter of 1862. This was the room or the school—for the room and the school were one—associated with the name of General Gordon.

div.head: GORDON'S_ GOLD MEDAL
div.p: GORDON'S_ GOLD MEDAL

It was in 1867 that General Gordon, or Lieutenant-Colonel Gordon, as he then was, came to Manchester. He was sent there On a political errand. The Reform Bill of 1867 gave a third member of Parliament to Man- chester, as well as to Liverpool. Birming- ham, and Leeds. But the increase in the number of Parliamentary representatives necessitated a fresh delimitation of the con- stituencies, and Colonel Gordon was entrusted with the duty of drawing up a report upon the boundaries of the new electoral divisions. One characteristic inci- dent of his life, an incident not then publicly known, had already connected him with Manchester. His biographer, Mr. Egmont Hake, relates it in the following words : "He had a great number of medals for which he cared nothing. There was a gold one, however, given to him by the Empress of China, with a special inscription engraved upon it, for which he had a great liking. But it suddenly idisappeared, no one knew where or how. Years afterwards it was found out, by a curious accident, that Gordon had erased the inscription and sent the medal anonymously to Canon Miller for the relief of the sufferers from the cotton famine at Manchester." ("The Story of Chinese Gordon," page 227.) The Canon Miller is presumably Canon Miller of Green- wich; there was no Canon Miller, reel- dentiary or honorary, then at Manchester. It was at a stormy time that Colonel Gordon came to Manchester. It was the year of the murd,r of Sergeant Brett and of the execution of three of his murderers— Allen, Larkin, and Gould. Their execution was followed in little more than a fortnight by the momentous explosion at the House of Detention in Clerkenwell. The anni- versary of their execution, November 23rd, is still celebrated as a memorable day by the Irish population of Manchester.

div.head: TEACHER AND PUPILS.
div.p: TEACHER AND PUPILS.

Colonel Gordon, however, did not trouble himself with politics. He lived for some six months in Manchester at the Queen's Hotel. He passed his days in surveying the city ; but he devoted his nights in Manchester, as afterwards at Gravesend, to work among the poor boys of the city. Soon after the arrival he paid a visit to the central office of the City Mission and expressed a wish to become a teacher in the Ragged Sehool. Mr. Johnson took him to Dark Lane. There he spent his evenings, teaching a class of poor rough boys, in a room so crowded that a good many of the children in the classes, which were all taught together, and in his class among the rest, were generally sitting or lying on the floor. Yet his labours were not in vain. His devotion touched the hearts of his humble pupils. When he left Man- chester for Liverpool, some of them went to bid him farewell at the station. One of these boys, a drayman still living in Man- chester, is fond of recalling his presence in the school and the scene at the station when he went away. It may be interesting to quote two or three passages from letters written by him after leaving Manchester to Mr. Johnson, with special reference to these

associations of his life there. "Remember me," he says in one of them, " to all 4ny friends, the lads of Dark Lane" ;and in another. "Believe me, yours sincerely, with kind regards to the dear lads in Dark Lane— Gravel, Alco4, Carr, %ape, and all the Shepleys. Jones. &c., &c." In another letter he sends Et for the Dark Lana School. From Gravesend he writes," I do remember those lads with such pleasure, and Ido believe that if all my dear friends could see it, they are all people of God." But the most touching of all the incidents in his life at Manchester must be told in Mr. John- son's own words. "One evening after I had been observing his patient endurance and perseverance with one or two reckless, inso- lent lade as we left the school, I, in a quiet, pleasant way, remarked, 'I fear, Colonel, yoUr Christian work in Dark Lane Ragged School will never get the fame and applause from this world that your military achieve- ments in China have lately secured for you.' "' My dear sir,' he replied, if I can but be the means in the hands of God of leading any of these precious souls to Jesus, I must place that among the most glorious trophies of my life, and to hear the Master at last say, "Inasmuch as ye have done it to one of the least of these, ye have done it unto me," will be to me a resplendent, undying glory, when so many of earth's fleeting honours, have tarnished and faded away into obscurity." This is the episode in General Gordon's life unknown to the world, and little known even to the citizens of Manchester; but it is not, I think, unworthy of a brief record. Perhaps it could at no time be more suitably recorded than on the anniversary of his deathday, January 28th, 1885.—" Manchester City News."

AT WHOSE HOME?

A beautiful little canary came flying by and settled down on the branch of a honey- suckle. "I'm so tired," he said. "I haven't found a really happy home ;,,et. I'm sure, though, that no one would be unkind or unhappy in such a charming Oace as this. I think I'll make my home here." But just then a dog came around the corner of the porch, limping and crying, for a boy was running after him, striking him cruelly with a big stick. "Oh oh" said the bird, and away he flew. "I couldn't stay there. That boy would surely be unkind to me." And he flew to a window sill of a fine stone house in a beautiful garden. "What a lovely home! I'm sure I can stay here." But there were sounds of crying from the room within, and, peeping in, he saw two little sisters quarreling over a doll. "Let go! That's my doll l" " No, you shan't have it. I want to play with it" ; and in the struggle the poor little doll was pulled to pieces. "Dear! Oh, dear r' chirped the poor little bird. "They might try to do that with me. I don't want to live here." _

On he flew, from home to home, finding unkindness so often that at last he sank down, worn out, onto a porch to die, his poor little heart almost broken with sadness. Suddenly he felt a warm hand close over him and a soft, kind, little voice said : " Why, you poor little thing! Oh, mother, see this dear little bird I Please let me keep him. take good care of him, and not let a thing hurt him I"
"Very well, dear, you may. Now go and feed him."
And the little canary found happiness and kindness at last, and sang and made the little child happy for being so good to him. Now if that bird had come to your house what would have happened?

The Bishop of Durham is very fond of dumb animals, and be tells a story of a little , lesson on kindness to dumb animals lie gave to a Sunday school class. "Now tell me," the Bishop asked one small child," why is it wrong to cut off little dogs' tails?" To which a damsel replied" Because of the text in the Bible." The Bishop was rather puzzled, because he had mentioned no particular text so far. "What text my dear?" She thought hard for a second, then she told him ' "What God bath joined together, let no man put asunder."

I think that in a general way the electors realise when they vote for a party man that they are voting not so much for the individual candidate who represents the party as for the party itself, and they send ' him to Parliament not so much to try to carry out his own individual opinions as to co-operate with the other members of his party in forwarding the general policy and aims of the party. While it may be true that a constituency admires a member who on occasions shows some independence of speech and action, it, as a general rule, looks to him to give his support to the general policy of the party even when that support requires him to vote against his own views. That members are sent to Parliament to act as party men can be proved to bathe practice, and the understanding by a thousand illus- trations if necessary. Every Unionist candi- date is a pledged follower of Mr. Balfour. He asks to be returned to support Mr. Balfour, and to co-operate with other Unionist members in following Mr. Balfour's lead. Every Liberal candidate is a follower of Mr. Asquith. On the eve of the General Election Mr. Asquith announced his election pro- gramme, and this became the programme of the Liberal party. The country, too, accepts the arrange- ment that the direction of Parliamentary business shall be in the hands of the Cabinet. This may be a good thing, it may be a bad thing. It may be that the country approves this concentration of authority in the hands of a Committee of a party called a Cabinet, elected by one man, or it may be that the country accepts it because it has never seri- ously thought about it at all. But the fact, nevertheless, remains, that with the consent of the electorate we are governed by Cabinet authority, and that Cabinet authority requires the support of the rank and file of the Parliamentary party. Ido not think it is for the Labour Party to quarrel with the principle of individual sub- ordination to party opinion. It was but a few weeks ago that the Constitution of the Labour Party required that every member should on all questions follow the Whip of the party. This is still nominally the policy of the Labour Party. It is a policy which can be defended by the unanswerable argu- ment that it is the only policy by which party government is possible and parties can be kept together. It is certainly not for the Labour Party to cast stones at a Liberal or a Tory who votes against his personal opinions to keep his party in office or because his party has decided upon a particular line of action.

div.head: FROM LABOUR'S STANDPOINT.
div.p: FROM LABOUR'S STANDPOINT.
By Philip Snowden, N P A QUESTION OF POLICY.

The Conference of the Independent Labour Party which met at Birmingham last week discussed a matter of the highest political importance. The Conference is to be congratulated upon the high ground from which it debated this vital question, and upon the freedom from personal imputations which characterised the discussion. The subject was whether a Labour Party in Parliament should vote on every question according to the merits of that one question or whether their action should be decided t./' a consideration of the relation of that ques- tion to collateral issues and by the effect which might be produced upon other interests by the result of the vote on the particular question. There is a very plausible case to be made out for the policy of voting on every ques- tion according to the merits of that question alone, and this case will appear to be conclusive to those who do not understand the system of Party government and of Cabinet responsibility.' It is a very frequent taunt against the partyl man that when he gets to Parliament he votes as his party leaders direct, and very often in violation of the pledges he has , given to his constituents at the election. As an illustration we may take the tea duty or the sugar tax. l'ractically every Liberal member is pledged to a reduction of these taxes. Most of the Liberal members who were elected in 1906 had given pledges to support the repeal of the sugar duty, and the reduction of the tea duty. But when pro- posals were brought forward to do these things, these members went back upon their pledges and voted against the reduction of the duties. They justified their inconsist- ency by the plea that to have voted for the reduction would have defeated the Govan,- ment, and that it was of more importance to keep in the Government than to get an immediate reduction of these taxes. In other words, they had not only given election pledges to remove the food taxes, but they were pledged also to support the Government and having to choose which of these pledges they would keep they chose to support the Government as the better course, all things considered, for them to follow. THE PARTY MAN.

div.head: FAULT OF THE SYSTEM.
div.p: THE FAULT OF THE SYSTEM.

So long as we have political parties we must have party government, and so long as we have party government we must have loyal support of the party from its members. If the Labour Party were in office in this country it is certain that they would exact as constant a support from their members as the other parties now do. The Australian Labour Party is disciplined with a rigour which is unknown to the Labour Party in this country. Therefore, we may take it as agreed that it is justifiable, and indeed necessary, that individual members should vote with their party on all vital issues, and should put the interests of their party before the fate of any single measure, believing that the whole for which the party stands is far greater than any one question or issue. But the indictment against a system of party government from the democratic point of view is not that it will not allow the expres- sion of individual opinions or per- mit freedom of individual action; the indictment is that under the existing system the members of a Parliamentary party are not permitted to share in formulating the programme of the party. The Liberal and Conservative members are merely " followers." They do not elect their leaders, they do not decide what questions the party shall take up. They go by deputations to their leaders to beg, cap in hand, that certain questions shall receive attention, and their leaders from a lofty eminence dispense or withhold their favours. There is no justification for exacting the support of the members of the party unless they have been consulted as to what should be done. The Cabinet should be in the position of a committee of a voluntary society, elected to carry out the work of the society, receiving its authority from the society, and responsible to the society; but subject to that, possessing full powers of administration, and having the right to claim the loyal support of the society so long as it is carrying out the general policy.

The Labour Party must suffer from the limitations which always accompany a minority position. The Labour Party can- not upset Party Government if it wished to do so. It cannot destroy the system of Cabinet Government. It might turn out one Cabinet, but another would be set up. The Labour members have been sent to Parlia- ment to help to get things done, and to make the best of the machinery available, and to try to improve it as the opportunity offers. But it would be simple madness to act as if conditions were not what they are but what we wanted them to be. The Labour Party will be doing a very useful work in showing up the anti-democratic character of the system of Cabinet despotism; and in agitat- ing for tin democratising of party govern- ment ; but it would be the height of folly to adopt a rigid policy of always voting on the merits of a particular question without regard to the effect which that action might have upon many other questions in which the Labour Party might have more at stake. Policy is a matter of balancing all the possible and probable consequences of a particular action, and the wise course of con- duct is to use the power which a minority may have in order to gain as much as possible from the majority which is in the seat of power. The Labour Party has made itself by preaching the doctrine that its independ- ence meant that it was independent to adopt such a policy as would force as much as possible 'from whatever Government might be in office. That is now its policy in Parlia- ment, and if for the time being it may be driven to support a Liberal Government to the extent of keeping it in office, although that Government is far from satisfactory in some respects, it is because that is the best of possible courses of action for the moment.

div.head: FRENCH PARALLEL.
div.p: THE FRENCH PARALLEL.

The position of a small group in a Parlia- ment which is governed on the party system by a Cabinet which "hangs together" is a very difficult one. The Labour Party are finding that to be the case. The difficulty was not apparent in the first Parliament because the Government majority was so great that the Labour Party could make no effect on that majority. But in this Parlia- ment it is different; and the question has to be faced as to what its policy should be. This was the question so power- fully debated at the I.L.P. Confer- ence. But no decision was reached, and that is not surprising, because it would pass the wit of man to lay down in precise terms what the policy should be which must be adhered to on all occasions. The British Labour Party is not alone in having this situation to face. At the French Socialist Congress last week, the same problem formed the main topic ofl discussion. The French Socialist party is al group among pqrties, and it may use its votes to turn out Ministries. They debated the question of how their votes should be used, and M. ,laures very eloquently upheld the very position which the British Labour Party has taken up of not committing itself to any rigid line of action, but of leaving itself free on all occasions to do what seemed the best, with the result that it sometimes votes on the merits of the question alone, and at other times takes collateral interests into account. MINORITY DIFFICULTIES.

div.head: LIFEBOAT INSTICUTION

Councillor Aineley presided over a lerge meeting at the Big Lamp, Widnes, on Saturday evening, called for the purpose of protesting against the action of the local Coronation Committee in placing an order for the Coronation cups to be supplied to the school children with a German firm. MR. J. A. SEDDON Al BURTON WOOD. Speaking at • meeting at Buttonwood on Saturday evening, Mr. J. A. Seddon, the Labour candidate for the Newton divieion, said Lord Wolmer was giving en idea that he was very busy in Parliament, and certain people who knew nothing about Parliamentary pro- cedure imegined (hat because be was asking • lot of questions he was doing a lot of work. But the asking of questione in the lions. of Commons was not an indication of the activity of the member. The Conservative party had a committee°, experts who drew up these questions and farmed them Gut to the members of Parliament connected with their party. If they happened to be aristocrats they got above their Mime, but if they belonged to the Honore of Cecil or were relativee of Lord Salisbury they would get a double share. (Laughter.) Lord Wollner had been conlerrined no a coward. He pot down a question about Mr. Marry Twist. Mr. Twist was acting for the Miners' Fede,ation, and if he did wrong be did no as the servant of the Federation. Lord %Wilmer shielded himself in • cowardly way behind the position of • member of Perliament,and put a question to the Attorney General, asking the Public Prosecutor to take criminal proceedings egninst Mr. Twist for carrying out hie dutiee as an official of the Miners' Federation. Ile asked that question in the name of a rival trade union, and he had no tight to shield himeelf as • member of the House of Commons. Had be done the same thing on the publio platform Mr. Twist could have taken proceedings against him under the law of conspiracy, hut became he happened to be member of Parliament he was free from all Lability.

Sir,—ln reply to your correapondenee 7Afore in sorrow than in anger,'"' may I point out that the Town Council Reaolution asking for a Women's Suffrage Bill on the lines of the Conciliation Bill was a favour fr.r these reasons -

(1). It in nct usual for the Town Council to pass Resolutions dealing with political affairs, and it was done on this occasion, Neal.° the Town Council felt that it was the oily representation sseembly of Men representing women's rotes. It was quite outside ordinary business.

The Councilor. Mho were willing to support the Resolution could in view of the length of the meeting, have decided to p stpone the matter. They did not because they knew it would be inconvenient to the National Union nct to have the Resolution before May sth. Sme Councillors. I Lelieve, btayed on at the meeting to see tie Resolution through, at great personal inconvenience. As for the conciliatory attitude of in men to men it is surely a hopeful feature of the Women's Suffrage mkt Fdion.

"With regard to your other correspondent, Mr. J. Beaumont, of Manchester. We are, of course, immemely flattered that he should think %Varrington worthy of his interference, end our letter, although, "extraordinary," worthy of Lis comment. We said the minds of the town councillors were made up on the suffrage que•tion before they came to the Town Council meeting that passed a resolution in favour of Women's Sullrsgerhis, says Mr. Beaumont, is an amazing admission. The town councillors never heard a word, it seems, either before or at the time of the resolution, against Women's Suffrage. Now this seems to me an extra- ordinary and amazing admission of Mr. Beaumont's. It is not one business to state the anti-suffrage ewe. Why don't ariti-auffragists dot' It looks uncommonly as if there were nothing to say against the suffrage, and no ore to say that nothing. As a Wartingtim gentleman once remarked, we have never met that orient wr m in. We are asked to contrast the conduct of the Town Council in Warrington. " unpardonable in a politic representative,- with the methods of the anti- Suffragists—or is it the conduct of the Suffrage Society that is to he contrasted ? That is not quite clear. Anti-Suffragists. Mr Beaumont tell on, have canvasted diatricts in England by postcard, with results gloriously anti, and it is reasonable, he says, to suppose that people who would not answer the pout- card were anti, too, because, of course, if tbey bad been Suffragists they would have lifted up their voice to say so. Stich suppositions are not arguments. of course. Mr. Beaumont, however, really realises that there is an energy and determination among Suffragists not to he found among Anti-Suffragists. Sr—i am not afraid to declare openly that I was I attracted to the Hippodrome lent week to see "la Afy desire to see her originated not from my love I art, but because of the various objections that have been raised by numerous watch committees and parsons Now I have a dispodtion for the curious, and my curiosity was aroused; hence the desire to see for myself what has received the goodwill if some and the enmity of others. Perhaps I shall he condemned because of this curiosity, but I firmly believe that curiosity gives birth to imagination, arab t pureness either is a sure sign of the progresa of the individual.

'rho whole performance of " La Milo" from beginninr to end ought not to awaken at.y but the most healthy emotions either of billy or mind. had " I,a 31i10 " worn a ".merry widow " hat or the latest and shmtest Parisian skirt, I feel that the inference would have been diffetent, but no such things were worn. Man glories in his strength, and woman in her beauty, and "La WO'S petformance in a triumph of artistic Tosir.g. I hat such perform- snore are created to make money I do not doubt, and without the least hesitation I siy that most pemle work for the love of gain, and still are deeply interested in their productions,aud great at tist,p .eta, sculptors, and even ministers sell their abilities in the best market. What wrong di Mr. MacSaghten and" La, Milo " in following their example ? Who sh mid We be continually called upon to exinaine stamen and painting., without haring the privilege of geeing upon the real ? flow else shall we make comparison ? If the nude or eetnintule is always objectional le then must vets art gallery in the land he closed ? If it is good to admire the sun, mountains, river., flowers, arid animals (and people travel thousands of miles t i find the best) it is not logical to hide away our own persons es if they were the production of the Devil. A pleasure-loving character will have pleamre of s, sin a et, and as minds vary, no must attractions at a theatre .vary....

For my own part I prefer to see "The rinse Musketeers," but it does nct follow that I shall imitate " Porthos" and get intoxica,ed or gamble my money away. I cannot believe that thousands of Warringtonians who visited the Hippodrome were prompted to do so from debased motives ; and if any are suffering from the pangs of self-reproach I trust they will find relief from this letter. I hold no brief for" La Milo." The Hector gsins nothing Ig a•guing ha p jot; but " La Milo" gains a free adverti,eineld. To all people who love arts and reason, I any consoler and digest ; then reject all that is doubtful and imperfect, and ever remember that things invented by man are insignificant when cornpired with Nature. In conclusion I say nothing of the doubtful passage, that occur in the great works of Shakespeare, Milton. Burns and Byron. Professor Huxley aptly eat s ;—"The man who is all morality and intellect, although lie coy be good and even great, is, after all only half a man. There is beauty in the moral world and in the intellectual world ; but there is also a beauty which is neither moral nor intellectual, the beauty of the world of art. There are men who are devoid of the power of seeing it. as there are men who are born deaf and blind, and the Inas of threie, as of thew, is simply infinite. There are others in whom it in an over- powering passion. Ilappy men, born with the productive, or at lowest, the appreciative, genius of the artist.—Yours, , The Vines, Orford, Warrington.
